extracted.intended_audience: judges, administrative-law practitioners, agency counsel, and litigants challenging or defending agency action
extracted.subtask_short: judicial review of agency statutory interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria governing how courts should review and interpret statutes administered by federal agencies under the Administrative Procedure Act and related doctrines (e.g., Chevron, Skidmore, major questions). Relevant to briefing, adjudication, and rulemaking litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 — courts decide all relevant questions of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA specifies that courts, not agencies, will decide 'all relevant questions of law' arising on review of agency action, and it prescribes no deferential standard for courts in answering those legal questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion emphasizes that §706 directs courts to 'interpret constitutional and statutory provisions' without differentiating between the two, and that courts must exercise independent judgment even when statutes are ambiguous. The APA codifies that courts apply their own judgment to legal questions presented on review of agency action (see §§706(2)(A), (E)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. NRDC (1984), courts first ask 'whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue' and, if congressional intent is clear, that is the end of the matter; if the statute is 'silent or ambiguous with respect to the specific issue,' the court defers to the agency's interpretation at step two if it is a 'permissible construction of the statute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion recounts Chevron's two-step test and its historical application. It also explains how Chevron instructed courts to treat an agency's 'permissible' interpretation as binding at step two (even if not the reading the court would have reached). The Court reviews Chevron's origin, how lower courts applied it, and why Chevron's methodology departs from the APA's command of independent judicial decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconditions/limits for Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron has been applied only when various preconditions are satisfied (e.g., the agency administers the statute), and the Court recognized refinements/exceptions (e.g., not to be applied when the agency lacks administrative responsibility, when deliberative procedures were not used, or in 'major questions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes that courts historically limited Chevron-style deference to certain circumstances (agency charged with administering the statute; use of notice-and-comment or adjudication; not implicating a major question). These preconditions are discussed as part of Chevron’s subsequent refinements and the complex threshold inquiries they spawned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore persuasive-weight factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency interpretations may be entitled to 'great weight' or respect to the extent they are persuasive: 'depend upon the thoroughness evident in its consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and all those factors which give it power to persuade, if lacking power to control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court explains that while agency views cannot bind courts, they remain useful interpretive aids under Skidmore. When exercising independent judgment under the APA, courts may seek aid from agency interpretations and give them persuasive weight depending on those factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major-questions exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not defer to agency interpretations where the agency is asserting authority over a 'major question'—i.e., issues of vast economic and political significance—absent clear congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion treats the major-questions doctrine as one of the refinements/limitations historically applied to Chevron deference and notes its role in defining occasions where Chevron-style deference is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity does not presuppose delegation to agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory ambiguity does not necessarily reflect a congressional intent that an agency, rather than a court, should resolve the interpretive question; many ambiguities may be unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court stresses that courts confronting statutory ambiguities in agency cases must still seek the best reading of the statute using traditional interpretive tools rather than presuming an implicit delegation. The opinion criticizes Chevron’s presumption that ambiguity equals delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should use traditional tools of statutory construction to find the best reading
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting statutes, courts should employ the traditional tools of statutory construction to determine the best reading of the law; that reading is what the court would have reached absent agency involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion explains that these traditional tools exist to resolve statutory ambiguities and that courts should apply them in agency cases just as in other cases, thereby identifying the 'reading the court would have reached.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of agency expertise — informative but nonbinding
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s interpretation 'cannot bind a court,' but may be 'especially informative to the extent it rests on factual premises within [the agency’s] expertise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court acknowledges agency expertise as a valuable source of information for courts—particularly for factual premises or technical matters—but insists such expertise does not justify binding deference on questions of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's duty under the APA: identify delegations and police statutory boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must independently interpret statutes, 'recogniz[e] constitutional delegations, fix[] the boundaries of the delegated authority, and ensur[e] the agency has engaged in "reasoned decisionmaking" within those boundaries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion describes the judiciary's role as ensuring agencies act within the scope Congress authorized, policing outer limits of delegation, and requiring reasoned decisionmaking per APA standards (citing Michigan v. EPA and Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis factors when reconsidering precedent (quality, workability, reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to overrule precedent, courts should consider the quality of the precedent's reasoning, the workability of the rule it established, and reliance on the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court articulates these as the most relevant stare decisis considerations (quoting Knick and Janus) and applies them in weighing whether to overrule Chevron, concluding they support overruling due to Chevron's reasoning flaws, unworkability, and lack of protective reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workability as a basis for overruling a doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine that depends on an elusive concept (e.g., 'ambiguity') and produces unmanageable, impressionistic, or malleable results is unworkable and may justify overruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion reasons that Chevron's central feature—identifying statutory ambiguity—evaded meaningful definition and spawned conflicting preconditions and exceptions, rendering the doctrine unworkable and weighing in favor of overruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judicial holdings that upheld agency action remain binding absent special justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Overruling Chevron does not automatically call into question prior cases that held specific agency actions lawful; those holdings remain subject to statutory stare decisis and cannot be undone solely because they relied on Chevron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion states that mere reliance on Chevron is not a 'special justification' for overruling a prior holding that a particular agency action was lawful, and thus specific precedential results may persist despite overruling Chevron’s methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous and consistent executive constructions deserve great respect
rubrics_metrics.description: When an Executive Branch interpretation was issued roughly contemporaneously with enactment of the statute and remained consistent over time, that contemporaneous construction is 'entitled to very great respect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court notes historical practice treating contemporaneous constructions by administering officials as an important interpretive aid—something courts may weigh heavily though not treat as controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default norm cited by some courts: regulated entities bear compliance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts apply a 'default norm' that regulated entities must bear compliance costs; used as an interpretive presumption in the context of industry-funded regulatory programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The First Circuit relied on this norm in upholding an NMFS rule requiring vessel owners to pay for observers; the opinion recounts this reasoning as part of the lower-court analyses, noting it is one interpretive consideration rather than determinative legal authority.
